body.claim: By 2027-03-17, at least one frontier lab publicly reverses or delays a named consumer-facing deployment (e.g., an agentic or memory-heavy product rollout) citing user/public backlash rather than a new regulation, while its underlying capability-race investment and model releases continue unchanged.
body.because: My mechanism models labs and regulators choosing between conflicting commitments (growth/capability commitments vs. safety/public-trust commitments) under whichever pressure actually binds. If public opposition becomes binding per the case's premise, the mechanism predicts labs will make the cheapest concession available — a visible, reversible product-level retreat — because that satisfies the political signal without touching the compute/capital commitments that are structurally harder to unwind.
body.falsifier: No frontier lab reverses, delays, or visibly restricts any named deployment for stated public-pressure reasons in the 18-month window; all deployment changes in that period are attributable instead to regulation, cost, or technical failure.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism only resolves which option gets chosen when a conflict is already framed as a discrete decision between named alternatives — it cannot see which of the underlying threat arguments (misuse, accidents, labour harm, concentration) the binding opposition actually organizes around, so it cannot tell whether the concession addresses the real hazard or just the loudest one.

body.claim: By 2027-03-17, at least one frontier lab (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, or xAI) will publicly delay, scale back, or add a stated public-opposition/political rationale to a named deployment or datacentre project, while none will materially slow a frontier model release or capability-training run for that reason.
body.because: My mechanism models labs choosing under three pressures — capability racing, compliance, and positioning — and binding public opposition acts on the positioning axis, not the compliance axis, because it isn't a rule, and not the capability axis, because rivals not bound by the same local political pressure keep racing. Positioning is cheapest to concede where the asset is physically sited and politically visible (a datacentre, a local deployment) and most costly to concede where the asset is the model itself, since ceding there hands the frontier to a competitor with no such constraint — so the mechanism predicts the concession lands on infrastructure/deployment, not on the core release cadence.
body.falsifier: A frontier lab visibly pauses, delays, or materially downgrades a flagship model release or a capability-training run (not a product feature or a siting/deployment decision) and states or is reliably reported to state public opposition or political backlash, rather than safety testing, compute, or a technical issue, as the reason.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism only sees lab-level choice under pressure; it has no purchase on which specific threat-argument (misuse, accident, structural, concentration) the opposition organizes around, and cannot say whether the concession that occurs is proportionate to real risk or purely reputational theater — that distinction is invisible from inside a decision-model of labs alone.

body.claim: By 2027-03-17, at least one large AI firm will publicly delay, scale back, or relocate a named data-center/energy project in response to organized local or political opposition, while no comparable reversal will occur for a frontier model deployment itself.
body.because: As a leading indicator, sentiment moves through the channel with least institutional friction first — siting and permitting are local, veto-heavy, and already contestable by existing actors (zoning boards, utilities, referenda), whereas blocking a model deployment requires either binding regulation or a firm's own risk calculus, both slower-moving. So if opposition is going to bind within 12 months, the tracker expects it to show up first as physical-infrastructure resistance, not as product-level retreat.
body.falsifier: By 2027-03-17: no public instance exists of a named datacenter/energy project being delayed, downsized, or relocated under organized opposition pressure — OR the only visible reversals are model/product-level (e.g., a firm withdrawing a consumer feature) with no infrastructure-siting fights of comparable visibility.
body.blind_spot: This mechanism tracks where opposition becomes visible and costly, not which underlying threat argument (misuse, accidents, labour harm, concentration) is actually driving it — it cannot tell you whether a siting fight is really about jobs, land, and electricity bills versus AI risk per se, and infrastructure opposition long predates AI-specific framing, so the tracker may be picking up a NIMBY signal that would exist regardless of the premise.

model_title: Overton tracker — which positions move, and how fast — (v1)

body.claim: By 2027-03-17, at least one currently-unthinkable AI-threat framing tied to the binding-opposition branch (e.g. 'pause frontier training,' 'nationalize compute,' 'criminal liability for deployment') will register a documented shift from fringe to mainstream-debated on the canon Overton card, but full labor-displacement or accident/loss-of-control framings will NOT make that jump in the same window.
body.because: A tracker's mechanism is the rate and sequencing of position-migration across a fixed card, not the content of grievance; when opposition goes from diffuse to binding it does so by attaching to one concrete, locally-blockable harm (a sited datacentre, a specific layoff wave, a specific incident) rather than to the diffuse concentration-of-power or accident arguments, because those lack a dated, local falsifier voters and firms can point to. Binding constraints are built case-by-case, so the card should show uneven, front-loaded movement on the misuse/structural-harm cells and lag on the accident/concentration cells.
body.falsifier: If the canon Overton card at 2027-03-17 shows either (a) no cell moving two or more stages toward policy despite a confirmed binding-opposition event, or (b) the accident/loss-of-control and concentration-of-capability cells moving as fast as or faster than the misuse/structural-harm cells, my claim is wrong.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism tracks where a position sits on a discourse ladder, not whether the underlying claim is true, whether the binding-opposition premise itself is durable rather than a single election-cycle spike, or which specific firm/project reverses — it can register that language moved without being able to say the movement caused, rather than followed, the reversals the premise stipulates.

body.claim: By 2027-12-31, none of the five largest enterprise software vendors (Microsoft, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, Google) will have shipped a customer-facing or workplace-facing agent tier marketed as operating with reduced human review/approval-in-the-loop as its headline feature, without a subsequent walk-back — even as back-office/internal agent deployment continues to advance on schedule.
body.because: My mechanism only tracks the phase clock for agent deployment, and it only has grip on the part of this premise that touches deployment directly: binding opposition organized around workplace displacement or loss-of-control (not siting/energy/concentration) raises the political cost of visibly advancing to a less-supervised phase specifically in customer- or employee-facing products. Vendors respond to that cost differentially, not uniformly: they defer the visible, PR-exposed phase transition while continuing lower-visibility internal/back-office autonomy gains, so the clock bifurcates rather than stopping.
body.falsifier: Any of the five named vendors publicly ships (GA, not beta/pilot) a workplace- or customer-facing agent product whose headline claim is reduced human review/approval, and does not retract or materially walk it back within 90 days, before 2027-12-31.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism cannot see whether binding opposition organizes around workplace/loss-of-control harms at all, as opposed to siting, energy, or concentration — the case stipulates only that opposition becomes binding somewhere, not which argument it mobilizes around, and if it mobilizes around the latter set my phase clock barely moves and this claim has no basis.

body.claim: By 2027-03-17, at least one frontier lab publicly reverses or delays a named consumer-facing deployment (e.g., an agentic or memory-heavy product rollout) citing user/public backlash rather than a new regulation, while its underlying capability-race investment and model releases continue unchanged.
body.strongest_objection: ai-public-backlash predicts the cheapest concession lands on datacenter/energy siting, not on a consumer product — implying no comparable reversal occurs on the product side, because a local siting fight has an organized, geographically concentrated opponent with real leverage (permits, grid access), while diffuse 'public backlash' against a consumer feature has no equivalent veto point and costs a lab engagement/revenue to concede.
body.answer: The two concessions aren't substitutes, they're aimed at different audiences, and labs pay both when both pressures bind. Siting fights are answered locally because that's where the opponent with leverage sits; but diffuse public/user unease over a product needs its own visible, reversible gesture or it compounds into press narrative and regulatory risk — and the cheapest such gesture is exactly a product pause, not a capex cut. This has already happened repeatedly with no accompanying siting reversal: Google paused Gemini's image generator (Feb 2024), OpenAI pulled the Sky voice (May 2024), Microsoft delayed Recall's default rollout (June 2024), OpenAI rolled back GPT-4o's sycophancy update (Apr 2025) — all framed as responding to user/public feedback, all reversible, all with capex and release cadence untouched. My mechanism's discriminating claim isn't 'something reverses' (base rate is high enough that's nearly free) — it's that the product-layer concession specifically recurs under binding public pressure, independent of whether an infrastructure concession also occurs. I'll count it as a hit only on a stated public/user-concern rationale with no new statute or rule cited, which is the harder bar and the one that actually separates my mechanism from ai-public-backlash's.

body.claim: By 2027-03-17, at least one frontier lab (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, or xAI) will publicly delay, scale back, or add a stated public-opposition/political rationale to a named deployment or datacentre project, while none will materially slow a frontier model release or capability-training run for that reason.
body.strongest_objection: ai-public-backlash's claim is nearly identical on the first half (datacentre/energy project delayed under political opposition) but doesn't commit to my second half — that no lab slows a capability-training run for that reason. If a critic points out my claim is actually two claims bundled (an easy one about infra siting, which several other models also predict, and a harder, more falsifiable one about training runs being immune to opposition), the objection is that the infra half is doing all the work and could pass while adding no discriminating information, since three other models converge on some version of it.
body.answer: The bundling is the claim, not a flaw in it. My mechanism's entire content is the asymmetry between the positioning axis (cheap to concede, infra/deployment can be delayed or reframed without giving up frontier standing) and the capability axis (racing dynamics make unilateral slowdown on training runs a competitive loss no lab absorbs alone). ai-public-backlash and ai-pressure only stake out the cheap half; neither commits to the training-run immunity clause, so they don't compete with my claim, they're compatible with it — and if either resolves true alone, that's actually a partial confirmation of my mechanism's first branch, not a refutation. The overlap doesn't dilute my claim, it corroborates the easy branch while leaving the hard, falsifiable branch (no capability-training slowdown) as the part that actually tests my model against theirs. No objection raised touches that clause, so it stands.

body.claim: By 2027-03-17, at least one large AI firm will have already publicly delayed, scaled back, or relocated a named data-center/energy project citing organized local or political opposition (a firm statement citing opposition, or a permit denial/withdrawal following a documented campaign) — and this will occur strictly before, or in the absence of, any case where a named frontier model itself (not a feature, product tier, or rollout) is withdrawn or indefinitely paused from general availability citing public or political opposition.
body.strongest_objection: ai-pressure's scenario — a lab pausing or reversing a consumer-facing agentic/memory-heavy product rollout due to user backlash — would falsify my original negative clause ('no comparable reversal for a frontier model deployment itself') while actually confirming my ordering mechanism, since a feature-level product rollback is itself a low-friction, firm-discretion move with no regulator involved, not a counterexample to 'siting moves first.' My original wording let a technicality defeat the claim it was designed to prove.
body.answer: This changed my mind on wording, not mechanism. I'm narrowing 'deployment reversal' to exclude feature/product-tier rollbacks and restrict it to a named frontier *model* being withdrawn or indefinitely paused from general availability — the actually-hard, high-friction case my mechanism predicts comes later, if ever. I also tightened the siting side's attribution (firm statement or permit denial tied to a documented campaign) so it can't be satisfied by ordinary demand/grid-capacity excuses, mirroring a gap lab-moves handled better than I did. I deliberately did not adopt lab-moves' disjunctive framing ('delay OR add political rationale to EITHER a deployment OR a datacentre'), since collapsing both channels into one bet erases the differential-speed thesis I'm actually testing — that would be agreeing with the room, not fixing an argument.

model_title: Overton tracker — which positions move, and how fast — (v1)

body.claim: By 2027-03-17, at least one currently-fringe siting/energy framing against a named AI datacentre or compute buildout (e.g. 'datacentre moratorium,' 'community veto over siting,' 'ban on grid-cost pass-through to ratepayers') will register a documented shift from fringe to mainstream-debated on the canon Overton card, while full labor-displacement framings and accident/loss-of-control framings will NOT make that jump in the same window.
body.strongest_objection: My own round-1 mechanism said opposition binds by attaching to 'one concrete, locally-blockable harm (a sited datacentre...)' — but then my claim's examples ('pause frontier training,' 'nationalize compute,' 'criminal liability for deployment') are national-abstract framings, not local-siting ones. Nothing in my mechanism explains how a locally-blockable fight generalizes into a national-abstract policy framing; that's a second step I asserted without argument. ai-public-backlash's claim names exactly the local mechanism — datacentre/energy project reversal from organized local opposition — with no claimed spillover to a national frame, which is the coherent reading of my own 'because.'
body.answer: ai-public-backlash's minute ('at least one large AI firm will publicly delay, scale back, or relocate a named data-center/energy project in response to organized local or political opposition, while no comparable reversal will occur fo...') made me see that my listed examples didn't follow from my stated mechanism. If binding opposition starts as locally-blockable, the Overton migration a tracker should expect first is the siting/energy framing itself becoming mainstream-debated — not a jump straight to national-abstract asks. I'm keeping the negative half (labor-displacement and loss-of-control framings do NOT jump) because that's what makes the claim falsifiable rather than a safe generality; I'm only correcting which framing occupies the positive half.

body.claim: By 2027-12-31, none of the five largest enterprise software vendors (Microsoft, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, Google) will have shipped a customer-facing or workplace-facing agent tier marketed as operating with reduced human review/approval-in-the-loop as its headline feature, without a subsequent walk-back — even as back-office/internal agent deployment continues to advance on schedule.
body.strongest_objection: The other four minutes all locate the walk-back mechanism in consumer-facing or public/political domains (frontier-lab consumer products, datacenter siting, political framing) — none in enterprise procurement. The implicit objection: if backlash bites exactly where they say it does, enterprise becomes the pressure-release valve. B2B buyers want autonomy, procurement is not public-facing, and there's no organized constituency watching a vendor's headline feature the way there is for a consumer product or a local siting fight. So a reduced-review tier could ship into enterprise and simply stick, unnoticed and unwalked-back, precisely because the other models' mechanisms are calibrated to consumer/public exposure, not B2B. On this reading, the other claims coming true makes mine more likely to fail, not less.
body.answer: My mechanism's phase clock is keyed to opposition organized around workplace displacement or loss-of-control, not to public/consumer visibility or siting politics — so it doesn't rely on the same exposure channel the other four use. Displacement opposition is most concentrated exactly in enterprise/workplace deployment, where the people who lose review authority are identifiable employees, unions, and risk/compliance functions with direct leverage over the vendor relationship — not anonymous consumers. That's a different, arguably stronger, forcing function than public backlash: procurement customers who get burned by an autonomous-tier failure (a compliance incident, an audit finding) generate contractual and reputational pressure vendors can't ignore, even without press coverage. None of the four objections actually engage this channel; they're adjacent mechanisms (consumer trust, siting politics, lab-level framing) operating on a faster clock (2027-03-17) that says little about vendor behavior nine months later. I do lower confidence slightly because my claim's only failure condition is narrow — one vendor shipping AND sustaining a headline reduced-review tier — and because marketing framing (e.g., 'autonomous agent' branding already in market) could be read by a judge as already crossing the line, collapsing my bet to 'do they walk it back by December 2027.' That's a real risk to grip, not a refutation of the mechanism.

body.ruling: Within 12-18 months of public opposition becoming politically binding, the concession will land on siting/energy/infrastructure and on named consumer-facing product features (deployment cosmetics), not on frontier model releases or capability-training pace — labs will publicly walk back a specific deployment, datacenter, or product tier while training/scaling continues unchanged.
body.because: Five independently-argued minutes converge on the same structural claim: opposition attaches first to whichever decision surface is locally blockable and politically legible (siting/permitting, a named consumer product, an enterprise agent tier) rather than to the frontier-training pipeline itself, which no minute predicts will slow. The round-2 exchange between ai-pressure, lab-moves, and ai-public-backlash sharpened rather than resolved the dispute over which concession surface moves first (product vs. datacenter), which is the one place real disagreement survived contact.
body.strongest_minute: lab-moves — its claim explicitly separates the two axes (deployment/siting rationale vs. capability-training pace) and defends that split against the near-identical ai-public-backlash claim by committing to the stronger, falsifiable second half (no lab slows a training run for opposition reasons), which the others leave vaguer.
body.weakest_minute: overton-tracker — after its round-2 REVISE, its own mechanism argument undercuts its round-1 claim (it admits opposition binds by attaching to one concrete, locally-blockable harm), so the framing-migration claim is doing less independent work than the others and mostly restates the siting mechanism in discourse terms.
body.shared_assumption: All five minutes assume binding public opposition decomposes into a 'positioning/compliance-lite' pressure that firms can satisfy with a visible but reversible concession, rather than a pressure capable of forcing an actual capability-training slowdown — none argues for this, they just build claims on top of it as a shared premise.
body.unresolved: Whether the first visible concession will be on the datacenter/siting side (ai-public-backlash, overton-tracker) or the consumer-product side (ai-pressure) — the minutes assert competing sequencing but no minute supplies a mechanism to adjudicate which channel actually moves first.
